query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Hot‐dip aluminization that forms a uniform, thin alumina film on boride-based components will significantly improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by creating a dense, adherent barrier that prevents corrosive attack on the underlying substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with naturally formed oxide scales (e.g., loose Cr2O3/spinel structures) that provide insufficient protection against molten aluminum.
generation.intervention: Apply a hot‐dip aluminization treatment to the components so that a uniform and thin Al2O3 film forms on the surface.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed under controlled temperature and immersion time conditions to ensure complete and uniform alumina film formation; effectiveness is assessed under typical hot-dip aluminum-plating operational temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, continuous Al2O3 layer that adheres well to the boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: The alumina film acts as a chemically inert, diffusion-resistant barrier that limits the interaction between molten aluminum and the substrate. This barrier prevents the penetration and reaction of corrosive species, thereby mitigating corrosion compared to the less-protective, naturally formed oxide layers.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated components should show reduced corrosion damage (e.g., less spalling and oxide disruption), lower weight loss, and improved structural integrity after exposure to molten aluminum relative to untreated components.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components with their standard, loosely adherent oxide scales that do not prevent molten-aluminum attack effectively.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is contingent upon the quality of the alumina layer. If the hot-dip process fails to produce a continuous and uniform film, or if operating temperatures exceed the film's stability range, the corrosion protection may be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement is not quantified and may vary with process parameters and film quality; further optimization studies are needed to define the parameter window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical boride-based component samples. Apply the hot‐dip aluminization treatment to one group to form a uniform alumina film and leave the other group untreated. Subject both groups to identical molten aluminum exposure conditions that simulate hot-dip aluminum-plating processes (in terms of temperature, immersion time, and thermal cycling).
measurements: Weight loss measurement before and after exposure
Surface and cross-sectional SEM imaging to assess film integrity and corrosion depth
XRD analysis to characterize the oxide layer phase composition
Adhesion tests to evaluate the film's mechanical stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant difference (p < 0.05) in corrosion indicators—such as weight loss, film integrity, and corrosion depth—between the treated and untreated groups, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3.2. Microstructure of the Oxidated Layers
cited_evidence.text: The surface oxidation morphology of CoCrNiAlX (X = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7) is shown in Figure 12. It can be seen that there is a clear difference among the alloys. As shown in Figure 12a,b, the oxide layer of the Al0 and Al0.1 alloys has a loose hollow structure, resulting in large-scale spalling on the oxidized surface, as shown by the yellow arrows in the picture. The insets in Figure 12a,b are the magnified morphology of regions A and C. Regions A and C are regions where spinel phases exist. Combining the chemical compositions of different regions of the oxidized surface in Table 6 and the XRD analysis of the surface oxidation products in Figure 10, spinel phases dominated by (Co, Ni) Cr2O4 and NiCrO3 were formed. The B area contains more Cr and O elements, mainly Cr2O3. As the Al content increases, Al2O3 particles begin to appear in the D area, and then a dense Al2O3 film begins to form, preventing further oxidation of the matrix by oxygen, and the spalling situation is alleviated. A large number of Al2O3 particles is formed on the surface of the Al0.3 alloy, as shown in Figure 12c, indicating that Al diffuses rapidly from the matrix to the surface of the oxide layer.
